entries.description: D-053 residual: corrective-action EDIT and CLOSE carry no idempotency key.
entries.currentState: CLOSED at §291 (D-053). EDIT is naturally idempotent and was proven so: every field is assigned absolutely, and a replayed request leaves the row byte-identical with zero duplicate side effects. CLOSE was NOT: the transition was idempotent but recordClosureIntelligence INSERTED a new outcome row on every request, so a lost-response retry wrote two outcomes for one closure — and because checkRecurrence counts rows in a window, a retry could manufacture a recurrence that never happened and escalate the customer's own action on its own duplicate. findLearnedFix promotes at TWO occurrences, so two retries could mint a learned fix from one event. Closure side effects now fire on the TRANSITION rather than the request; close() had no gate at all. Proven: retry leaves outcomes at 1, and a genuine reopen-then-reclose still records a second outcome (1 -> 2), so it is not over-corrected.
entries.remediation: Extend the clientRequestId pattern to the two mutation routes, OR accept last-write-wins and state it. This is a PRECONDITION for any future offline outbox, not a live defect: no duplicate has been produced by either route.
entries.retestRequirement: A duplicate-submission measurement on both the edit and close routes.

entries.remediation: Do not add the migration. Decide what to do about the table that is already there — see DB-4, which carries the consequence.
entries.retestRequirement: Tied to DB-4 and TI-2.
entries.note: Status moved from BLOCKED to OPEN at §289 because the blocking premise was factually incorrect.

entries.description: No evidence exists of a tested backup or a rehearsed restore for the production database or object storage.
entries.currentState: The register recorded "no restore evidence in verification/". That was WRONG — §269 had already taken a backup and rehearsed a restore. §289 repeated it freshly and more strictly against live production: 14.4s, 7810853 bytes, 76 tables, 7051 rows; restored into a disposable PostgreSQL 17.11 target in 1s with 0 errors; verified by per-table content checksum, not row count. All 76 tables content-identical, digest da17e9b755a540dac240c5f2bd8c7a7c on both sides.
entries.remediation: Establish the backup schedule and retention, then rehearse one full restore to a disposable target and record the timing.

entries.note: The PLATFORM retention window is a separate question and is now BR-2. What is closed here is that an operator-controlled backup exists and restores correctly.

entries.description: Structured operational events are emitted to stdout/stderr with redaction, but there is no aggregation, alerting, error tracking or incident runbook.
entries.currentState: MECHANISM IMPLEMENTED AND PROVEN; NO DESTINATION CONFIGURED IN PRODUCTION. §291 built the push half MO-1 asks for: every error-severity operational event is dispatched to a configured destination, repeated 5xx raise ONE service.error_rate_exceeded rather than one alert per request, and one alert per event kind per 15-minute window keeps an outage from becoming a mail storm. Proven against a real induced storage failure: six consecutive 500s produced THREE alerts — one per event kind plus one rate alert — while 401, 404 and 400 produced none, which is the noise policy §291 specified. §291 did NOT invent a production destination, because choosing an alerting channel has a cost and an account attached. /health/ready now reports alerting: NOT_CONFIGURED, so "nothing is watching" is a visible fact rather than a silent assumption. THIS IS NOT YET MONITORING IN PRODUCTION. §292 SEARCHED FOR AN EXISTING DESTINATION AND FOUND NONE. Project documentation names exactly one established operational destination — the Render service notification (notifyOnFail, email to the workspace owner) — and that is a PLATFORM channel for deploy and service failure that the application cannot publish into. There is no Slack, PagerDuty, Sentry or webhook configuration anywhere in the repository or either platform; Render has zero webhooks and no log stream; and the Resend credential that would enable the email channel does not exist (EM-2). §292 did NOT invent a destination. The noise policy was re-proven on the §292 build against a real receiver: 401, 404, 400, duplicate-register and 402 produced ZERO alerts, while one qualifying 500 produced two alerts — one per event kind — delivered in 4 ms with metadata carrying no content.
entries.remediation: MONITORING_DESTINATION_OWNER_DECISION_REQUIRED. The product owner must name a destination: either a webhook URL for a receiver they control (a Slack incoming webhook is the cheapest), or an alert email address together with a Resend credential (which also closes EM-2). Configuration is then one environment variable and one induced failure to confirm receipt.
entries.retestRequirement: An induced error-severity event arriving at the configured destination, and /health/ready reporting alerting: configured.

entries.description: Privately authored consensus standards (ANSI, ASTM, NFPA, ANSI/ASSP) are referenced by NAME AND TOPICAL SCOPE ONLY. No standard text is reproduced anywhere in the shipped product.

entries.remediation: This is the correct posture and must be PRESERVED as a hard rule. ASTM v. Public.Resource.Org (D.C. Cir. 2023) held that NON-COMMERCIAL posting of incorporated-by-reference standards is fair use; the standards remain copyrighted and that holding does not extend to a COMMERCIAL product redistributing the text. Incorporation by reference does not make private standard text freely redistributable here.

entries.description: No production acceptance procedure is defined: after deploying, nothing states what must be true before a human is allowed to use the system.
entries.currentState: EXECUTED at §291 against the deployed release. Consent-gated registration, login, session, site, inspection, observation, user-authored finding, human review, finalization, completion readiness, in_review and completed transitions, corrective-action create, update and CLOSE, calendar, report generation, checksum-matched download, revision identity, logout, fresh login, and persistence of every authoritative record across the new session. entries.description: The cross-tenant recurrence path is REACHABLE in production, because the outcomes table exists there although no migration creates it.
entries.currentState: REPAIRED AND PRODUCTION-SHAPE VALIDATED at §291. Root cause was not the missing table: §289 found the table present, and §291 measured why — TypeORM synchronize created it, along with twenty other entity-derived tables, before the switch was turned off. The defect was an unscoped query. checkRecurrence now joins outcomes to corrective_actions and applies the product's own workspace predicate (organizationId, or organizationId IS NULL plus ownerUserId), and the scope is a REQUIRED argument so a recurrence figure cannot be computed without one. No column was added to a table outside the migration lineage. Validated on a production-SHAPED database — the clean rebuild plus production's own outcomes DDL, verified identical column-for-column — across two workspaces: A influences A (true, escalated to urgent as intended); A cannot influence B (false, B stays medium); B cannot influence A (false); zero history correct; no identifier escapes. Negative control: the OLD query evaluated for B returns 1 row and would have set recurrence true. Deployed and exercised in production: a real closure wrote a clean outcome with recurrenceDetected=false and emitted no failure event.
entries.remediation: Either scope the recurrence query to tenant/workspace and prove both directions (the TI-2 remediation), or decide the outcome loop is deliberately global and make that a stated product position. A third option — dropping the production table to restore the original containment — is a production write and belongs to its own authorised section.
entries.retestRequirement: The two-workspace proof on a production-shaped database, including the negative control, on any change to the recurrence path.
entries.note: A second consequence: all §286 and §287 action-closure evidence was gathered against databases WITHOUT this table, so local closure evidence does not represent production closure behaviour. §290 PRODUCT-OWNER HOLD: DB-4 is REAL and must not be described as unreachable. It does NOT block Threshold A, which authorises deployment rather than ordinary product use. It DOES block unrestricted Threshold B corrective-action operation and External Beta. Until it is repaired and production-shape validated, corrective-action CLOSURE must not be exercised in production except as a deliberately bounded synthetic release test, and §290 determined such a test was not essential and did not perform one.

What is establishable from an authenticated SQL client was recorded: provider Neon, PostgreSQL 17.11, region us-east-1, endpoint ep-weathered-moon-a4egk93d, branch br-misty-union-a4uke5p1, timeline ee18de24df1cae2c62e918f771e9e88c, compute compute-small-dream-a4z4u8tu, max_cluster_size 512. The history-retention window, the PITR window and the plan are CONTROL-PLANE settings and are not exposed to SQL. Routes exhausted: neonctl not installed and no ~/.config/neonctl; no NEON_* environment variable; zero Vercel marketplace integrations (a Neon integration would have carried a key); no API key anywhere; and the neon.* GUCs expose identity, not retention. WHAT IS NOT IN DOUBT is the operator-controlled backup path, now proven three times (§269, §289, §291) including a fresh backup and a full content-checksum restore immediately before the §291 migration.

entries.description: No Node version is pinned, and the Render runtime Node version cannot be read.
entries.currentState: CLOSED at §292. The production runtime was not observable, so §292 made it observable first rather than pinning a guess: /health/version now reports process.version at request time and whether the repository declares a pin. It did not need a deploy to discover the version — the Render build log states it: "Using Node.js version 24.14.1 (default)". BOTH production halves already ran Node 24 (Render 24.14.1 by default, Vercel 24.x by project setting), so the pin makes an implicit default explicit rather than changing what executes. engines.node ">=24.14.1 <25.0.0" in both packages plus backend/.node-version 24.14.1 so Render resolves exactly; no .nvmrc, which would be a third declaration of the same fact. Proven on that exact runtime installed locally: clean npm ci in both packages with ZERO EBADENGINE warnings, backend tsc, frontend tsc --noEmit, next build 25/25, and all 15 gates. Verified in production after deploy: the build log now reads "via /opt/render/project/src/backend/.node-version" and the running process reports nodeVersion v24.14.1 with nodeVersionPinned ">=24.14.1 <25.0.0".
entries.remediation: Add engines.node to both packages and a NODE_VERSION variable on the Render service, then re-read and record the runtime version.
entries.retestRequirement: A production /health/version read where nodeVersion satisfies nodeVersionPinned.
entries.note: §289 reported the gates running on Node v20.20.2; they were in fact on v26.7.0 after a PATH change moved `node` to the Homebrew build. That drift is exactly what this pin closes.

entries.description: NEXT_PUBLIC_DISABLE_AUTH is scoped to the Vercel PRODUCTION environment.
entries.currentState: STRUCTURALLY INERT TODAY, and registered anyway. Every consumer either tests NODE_ENV !== "production" directly (AppShell.tsx:3, lib/auth.ts:113, lib/billing.ts isLocalDevAuthBypass) or delegates to getLocalDevPlanCode(), whose first line returns "free" when NODE_ENV === "production". So the variable does nothing in a production build whatever its value. The hazard is the next consumer who reads the variable without the guard.

entries.description: Learned corrective-action fixes were selected across every tenant and surfaced in HazLenz proposals.
entries.currentState: CLOSED at §292, and the §291 repair was itself corrected to get there. §291 added an OPTIONAL `scope` parameter and returned early when it was absent — but the query underneath was never scoped, so the guard held only because no caller passed a scope and would have become FAIL-OPEN the moment one did: the caller would have believed it asked for one workspace and received every workspace. The parameter is removed. There is now no way to ASK for cross-tenant data. PROVEN on production-shaped data with fix_feedback populated from two workspaces: the OLD query returns BOTH workspaces' confidential remediation wording; the current one returns nothing; forcing an extra argument still returns nothing; and the real HazLenz read path — the actions it would propose — contains neither workspace's wording. Writes retained (4 rows).

entries.description: Closure intelligence failed for every hand-created corrective action.

Verified in production: a real closure wrote a clean outcome row and emitted no failure event.

entries.description: Production has no Resend credential, so password reset cannot deliver.
entries.currentState: PASSWORD_RESET_PROVIDER=resend in production, but RESEND_API_KEY and PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL are both ABSENT from the 41 production environment variables. checkProductionConfiguration() is written to require all three, yet the service starts — so the check is not enforced as a boot refusal. Consequence: a user who forgets their password cannot recover it. It also removes the most obvious destination for MO-1 alerting. §292 checked for an already-owned credential rather than creating one: no RESEND_API_KEY in any local env file, none in the environment, and none in production. Configuring it would require creating an account and accepting terms on the owner's behalf, which §292 forbids. Left OPEN. It does not block Threshold B — password reset is recoverable for an internal owner — but it does block the email option for MO-1.
entries.remediation: Configure RESEND_API_KEY and PASSWORD_RESET_FROM_EMAIL, then exercise one password reset end to end. Separately, decide whether the boot contract should REFUSE rather than merely report.
entries.retestRequirement: A password reset requested and received.

entries.description: Workspace-scoped learning from corrective-action outcomes is not implemented and is not a v1 capability.

Making it work needs a workspace column on fix_feedback populated at write time and a scope threaded from the HazLenz analysis pipeline, which carries none today. That is a migration plus a pipeline change and a product decision about whether the loop ships at all.
entries.remediation: Product decision. If it ships: add the column, populate it, thread the scope, and prove both directions as DB-4 was proven. If not: remove the read path and stop writing.
entries.retestRequirement: A two-workspace regression proving same-workspace feedback CAN influence a proposal and other-workspace feedback CANNOT.
entries.note: Carried as DEFERRED, not as a defect: there is no cross-tenant path left to close. DB-5 closed that.

thresholdCountRule: A threshold's blocker count is the number of entries whose blocksThresholdX flag is set. Closing an entry clears its flags and records what it used to block in wasBlockingThresholds, so the entry is never deleted and the count never counts a closed item.
candidateHeadNote: The release SHA is the branch tip at push time and CANNOT be recorded inside the commit that would record it — each such commit changes the value. So the release is bound by a digest instead of by a SHA, which is the stronger binding in any case: the SHA to deploy is whatever origin/beta/expert-hazlenz-validated-candidate-2026-09-12 points at after step 1, PROVIDED its applicationSourceDigest equals 2ce8a1d7b045818cb9708af9414fe8d189523e334dad955b617268cc932f2618. Verify that before deploying; it is one command.
